new_statements.quote: Stress by default occurs on the penultimate syllable, although there are some examples of contrastive stress to encode semantic difference. One such minimal pair includes /kɑˈwam/ 'your mouth' and /ˈkɑwam/ 'your spouse'.
new_statements.citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Ghayavi language', English Wikipedia, rev. 1330828531 (2 Jan 2026), section 'Phonology' (paragraph added 25 Apr 2023, rev 1151626233, anonymous IP 150.203.68.92; underlying primary source not named)
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; a small number of lexical items carry non-default (contrastive) stress, e.g. final-stressed kaˈwam 'your mouth' vs penult-stressed ˈkawam 'your spouse'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'some examples of contrastive stress to encode semantic difference' — minimal pair /kɑˈwam/ 'your mouth' vs /ˈkɑwam/ 'your spouse'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, unspecified whether citation forms; the only cluster-level primary remark (Lithgow 1976: 475, PTC-wide) says stress is predictable within word classes and shifts one syllable rightward when kin-plural or object suffixes are added, but gives no Ghayavi-specific placement rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Ghayavi = Boianaki/Boanaki (Lithgow 1976: 'Boanaki (Galavi)', coast from Uga to Vidia, centre Boanaki; 75% dialect variation Boanaki-Vidia) = Ray 1907 'Galavi' (Boianai village). Wikipedia's statement does not name a dialect. Glottolog places Ghayavi with Gapapaiwa in a Boanaki-Paiwa node (boan1246); no sister-language statement was used.

Only citation is a generic reference to Lynch, Ross & Crowley 2011 (The Oceanic Languages), which is cited for 'typical of most Oceanic languages', not for the stress claim; the primary source of the paragraph is not named.

sources.citation: Lithgow, David R. 1976. Austronesian languages: Milne Bay and adjacent islands (Milne Bay Province). In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 441-523. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: Sec. 84 'Stress', p. 475, is a Papuan-Tip-Cluster-wide survey remark: stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima (probably Nimowa, Sud-Est); 'In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs' (stress moves one syllable rightward with kin plural and object suffixes). Nothing specific to Boanaki/Ghayavi; no placement rule given.
